public_rationale: Customer token prices and provider serving expenses are different quantities. NIST explicitly distinguishes them, and research identifies both economic and technical influences on price declines. A lower price alone therefore does not establish a lower serving expense. This does not establish that OpenAI's particular price cut lacked an efficiency improvement.
limitations: The evidence does not measure OpenAI's private serving expenses around its o3 price cut.
Real efficiency improvements can accompany falling prices.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Falling token prices do not mean the cost of serving tokens has fallen.

statement.excerpt: The cost of tokens is not the same as the cost of serving tokens!
statement.document_title: The Subprime AI Crisis Is Here

our_interpretation: In context, 'cost of tokens' means the price customers pay, while serving cost means the provider's production expense.
The ordinary reading is that a price reduction alone does not establish a reduction in production expense. It does not assert that serving costs never fall.
The surrounding discussion uses 2025 pricing examples and describes practices continuing at publication. Assess that contextual period through March 31, 2026.
criteria.support_condition: Authoritative definitions or research distinguish customer token prices from provider serving expenses and establish that pricing changes can reflect factors other than production efficiency.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence establishes that customer token prices necessarily track provider serving expenses, so a price decline itself establishes a serving-cost decline.
